analysis.one_liner: Exempted nearly all federally funded construction projects from federal prevailing-wage rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House subcommittee and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law (the Davis-Bacon Act) requires contractors on federally funded construction to pay local prevailing wages, which typically means union-scale pay. This bill would have raised the contract-size threshold for coverage from $2,000 to $500,000, exempting almost every federal construction contract, and redefined prevailing wages using the full range of local pay rather than the most common rate. It also would have let contractors substitute lower-paid semi-skilled helpers for journeyman mechanics. The bill carried a few worker-protective pieces — back wages paid directly to workers and penalties for splitting contracts to dodge the law — but its main effect was to allow lower pay on federally funded construction.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors on federal projects, especially nonunion open-shop firms, who could pay market rates instead of prevailing union-scale wages and face less payroll paperwork. The bill's stated goals also included savings for federal taxpayers and more room for small and minority contractors to compete.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nonunion construction contractors bidding federal work

how_it_helps.text: Raises the Davis-Bacon coverage threshold from $2,000 to $500,000, exempting the vast majority of federal and federally assisted construction contracts from prevailing-wage requirements.

Redefines prevailing wage as the 'entire range of wages' paid to a worker class in a smaller urban or rural subdivision, and excludes wages on federal projects from the calculation — mechanisms that tend to pull required rates toward the lower end of local pay.
Creates a separate semi-skilled 'helper' classification, letting contractors pay helpers below journeyman rates for work assistants currently perform.
Reduces Copeland Act payroll reporting from weekly statements to three statements per contract, cutting contractor paperwork.
Requires back wages owed to laborers and mechanics to be paid directly to the workers from withheld contract payments, and penalizes splitting projects into smaller contracts to evade the wage rules.

analysis.who_pays: Laborers and mechanics working on federally funded construction, who would earn less as prevailing-wage protections shrink; union building trades whose wage standards underpin federal construction pay also lose bargaining ground.

drawbacks.text: Wages for workers on federal projects would fall, because the bill both exempts most projects and redefines the prevailing wage toward the full range of local pay rather than the most-common rate.
The semi-skilled helper classification would shift work now done by journeyman mechanics to a lower-paid class, reducing skilled workers' hours and earnings.
Cutting payroll certification from weekly to three times per contract weakens the paper trail used to verify that workers actually received required wages.

The bill's own design concedes uncertainty: it orders the Labor Secretary and Comptroller General to report annually on the effects on local wages and the economy, acknowledging the claimed savings were unproven.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings would come mostly out of construction workers' paychecks rather than out of contractor margins, since the bill lowers required wages and cuts reporting. Its taxpayer-savings case is disputed, and the bill itself mandates annual federal studies of the wage and economic effects — an honest supporter would admit the outcomes were untested. The direct back-pay and anti-contract-splitting provisions are genuine worker protections, but they sit inside a bill whose headline effect is a much smaller share of federal construction covered at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, sent down to its labor standards subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Stenholm (D-TX) and five original cosponsors introduced the Davis-Bacon Reform Act on May 6, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
On May 27, 1993, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety, where no further action was recorded.
The bill gathered 25 cosponsors, 22 Republicans and 3 Democrats, but never received a committee or floor vote in the 103rd Congress.
The measure died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, leaving Davis-Bacon coverage unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, construction workers on federally funded projects kept prevailing-wage protections, and union-scale pay standards survived intact. Contractors who would have paid lower wages on federal jobs did not get the exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers kept their wage floor

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan in a skewed way — a Texas Democrat leading, with 22 Republicans and 3 Democrats cosponsoring — but no votes were ever taken, so the bill's real partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would let them bid federal work without paying prevailing (union-scale) wages and with far less payroll paperwork. Their labor-cost savings come directly out of the paychecks of workers on those projects.

industries.industry: Union building trades and union-signatory contractors
industries.note: Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage determinations anchor union-scale pay on federal construction. Exempting nearly all federal contracts and allowing cheaper helper classifications would undercut the wage standards that union contractors and their workers compete on.

The bill's stated purpose is to expand their participation in federal contracting by lifting wage rules and paperwork on smaller contracts. The opportunity comes bundled with a lower-wage workforce, so the benefit to these firms rests on the same mechanism that cuts worker pay.
